title: Inferences and conclusions about purpose and meaning
blurb: Read between the lines: combine text clues with reasoning to reach the conclusion the passage best supports.
question: A short passage says a man reread a letter, ironed his new scrubs twice and left for a ten-minute drive forty minutes early. The question asks what the reader can infer. One option repeats that he left early; another says he dislikes driving. What is the correct inference, and why are those two options wrong?

teach.body: Formally, an inference is a logical conclusion based on evidence in the text plus reasoning, rather than something stated directly. Drawing a conclusion means combining several details to reach a judgment the author implies: a purpose, an attitude, a likely cause or an audience. In plain English: the text gives you the clues, you connect them, and the best inference is the one the clues most strongly support, not just one that could be true.

Leon set his backpack by the door before his alarm went off. He reread the acceptance letter taped to the refrigerator, ironed his new navy scrubs a second time and checked that his badge was clipped to the pocket. Although the hospital was a ten-minute drive away, he left forty minutes early.

Nothing here says 'Leon is nervous and eager about his first day.' But every detail points to it: waking before the alarm, rereading the letter, ironing twice, leaving very early.

head: Clue type
Example from the passage
rows: Ironed the scrubs a second time
The acceptance letter on the fridge
Ten-minute drive, left forty minutes early
teach.caption: Tone, examples and cause-effect signals (because, so, as a result) are clues too.

rows.label: Example
values: He is eager about the new job

teach.body: Many TEAS inference items ask why, not what. Why did the author include this detail? What does this paragraph add? What does this figure of speech suggest? Who is the intended reader? A leaflet that speaks to 'you', uses short numbered steps and says 'bring this card to every visit' was written for patients, even though it never says so. Answer from the clues, never from what you happen to know about the topic.

items: Spot the signal in the stem: infer, suggest, imply, most likely, conclude.
Find the lines the question is about and reread them.
Ask: given these lines, what must be true or is most strongly supported?
Eliminate options that are stated outright, extreme (always, never, all), based on outside knowledge or unsupported.
Choose the option that every relevant detail supports and none contradicts.

teach.h: How strongly does the text support it?
teach.caption: The correct answer sits at the top of this scale. 'Could be true' is level 2, and it is a trap.

teach.text: Four inference traps: (1) an option that is directly stated, which is locating, not inferring; (2) an extreme option with all, never, always or proves; (3) an option that relies on outside knowledge or personal opinion; (4) reversed cause and effect. If you cannot point to the clues behind an option, do not choose it.

teach.body: Keisha Morgan, applying to a practical nursing program, reads a clinic memo: 'Starting Monday, flu shots will be given in Room 4 only. Please direct walk-in patients there and remind them to bring their insurance card.' Asked about the audience, she notices 'direct walk-in patients there': the memo is written for front-desk staff, not patients. Nothing says 'to staff', but the clues require it.

items: Inference = evidence in the text + reasoning; not stated directly.
The best inference is the most strongly supported one, not merely a possible one.
Clues: actions, details included or left out, word choice, tone, examples, cause-effect signals.
Inference items also ask about purpose, meaning of a phrase and intended audience.
Reject stated facts, extreme words, outside knowledge and reversed cause and effect.

summary: You can now draw inferences and conclusions by connecting text clues with reasoning, including inferences about an author's purpose, a phrase's meaning and the intended audience. You can rank options by strength of support and reject stated, extreme, outside-knowledge and reversed options.

A.q:
Read the passage.

The waiting room clock read 4:52. Mr. Okafor had already paged through every magazine on the table twice, and he looked up each time the door to the exam rooms opened. When his name was finally called, he stood so quickly that his chair scraped the floor.

What can the reader infer about Mr. Okafor?
options: He arrived late and missed the time of his original appointment.
He is angry at the receptionist for calling other patients first.
He has been waiting a long time and is eager to be seen.
He has to wait longer than other patients at every visit.
A.why: Reading every magazine twice, watching the door and jumping up when called all point to a long wait and eagerness to be seen. Every clue supports it, and none contradicts it.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the passage mentions when he arrived or what time his appointment was.
whyNot.1: Overreach: impatience is supported, but the passage gives no sign of anger at the receptionist.
whyNot.3: Extreme: the passage describes one visit and cannot support a claim about every visit.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Bring this card to every visit. Write down any new medicine you start, including vitamins and herbal products. If you see more than one doctor, show this card to each of them, even if you think they already know what you take.

The author most likely wrote this passage to:
options: warn patients that herbal products interfere with medicines
persuade patients to see a single doctor for all of their care
help patients keep each provider aware of everything they take
explain to doctors how to record the vitamins a patient takes
A.why: Every instruction (bring the card, list everything including vitamins, show it to each doctor) serves one purpose: making sure all providers know everything the patient takes.

whyNot.0: Herbal products are listed as things to record; the passage never says they interfere with anything.
whyNot.1: The passage assumes patients may see more than one doctor and tells them what to do; it does not argue against it.
whyNot.3: The card is addressed to patients ('you'), not doctors.

A.q:
Read the passage.

When the new office manager arrived, the old routines were swept out with the dust. On her first morning, staff who had used the same paper forms for twenty years were handed tablets, and the weekly meeting moved from Friday afternoons to Monday mornings.

The phrase 'swept out with the dust' suggests that the old routines were:
options: quickly removed as outdated
cleaned up and kept in use
slowly phased out over years
stored with the old paper forms
A.why: Dust is something old and unwanted that is cleared away. The details (tablets on the first morning, the meeting moved) show the change was fast. So the routines were removed quickly as outdated.

whyNot.1: Sweeping something out means getting rid of it, not keeping it.
whyNot.2: The changes happened on her first morning, not over years.
whyNot.3: This reads the phrase literally; nothing says the routines were stored anywhere.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Carla has worked night shifts at the care home for six years. She keeps a spare pair of shoes in her locker, knows which residents like the radio on at 3 a.m., and is the person new staff are told to ask when something goes wrong.

Which of the following is an inference rather than a stated fact?
options: Carla has worked night shifts at the care home for six years.
Carla keeps a spare pair of shoes in her locker at the home.
Carla prefers night shifts to day shifts at the care home.
Coworkers regard Carla as experienced and dependable.
B.why: No sentence says coworkers see Carla as dependable, but new staff being told to ask her when something goes wrong, plus her six years and detailed knowledge, strongly support it.

whyNot.0: This is stated directly in the first sentence, so it is a fact from the text, not an inference.
whyNot.1: This is stated directly in the second sentence.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: working nights for six years does not show she prefers them; the passage never compares shifts.

B.q:
Read the passage.

In the first week of the hospital's new badge system, a line of about 20 people formed at the east entrance every morning at 7:00, when the day shift arrives. The west entrance, used mostly by visitors after 10:00, had no line at any time.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Many staff arriving at one entrance at once caused the line.
The badge readers at the east entrance were not working properly.
Visitors avoided the new badge system by using the west entrance.
Visitors slowly learning the badge system caused the east line.
B.why: The line appeared at the time and place where the day shift arrives, and nowhere else. The best-supported conclusion is that many staff badging in at once caused it.

whyNot.1: Nothing suggests a fault; the timing points to crowding, not broken equipment.
whyNot.2: The passage says visitors use the west entrance after 10:00; nothing suggests they were avoiding the system.
whyNot.3: Visitors mostly use the west entrance after 10:00; the east line formed at 7:00, when the day shift arrives.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Keep this sheet on your refrigerator. If your child's temperature reaches 100.4°F or higher, call our nurse line before giving a second dose of fever reducer. Do not give adult tablets to a child. Use the measuring cup that comes with liquid medicine, not a kitchen spoon.

Who is the most likely intended audience?
options: Nurses who answer the clinic's nurse line
Pharmacists who prepare children's medicine
Older children who take their own medicine
Parents or caregivers of young patients
B.why: The sheet speaks to 'you' about 'your child', tells the reader to call the nurse line and to keep the sheet at home. Those clues point to parents or caregivers.

whyNot.0: The reader is told to call the nurse line, so the reader is not the nurse who answers it.
whyNot.1: Advice to keep the sheet on the refrigerator and use the dosing cup is aimed at home use, not pharmacy work.
whyNot.2: The sheet refers to 'your child', so it addresses an adult responsible for a child.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Dr. Lena Ortiz spent the summer testing water from 40 private wells across Harlan County. She found that 9 of them contained nitrate levels above the federal limit, most of them near large farms. In her report, Dr. Ortiz notes that she grew up drinking water from one of those wells.

The author most likely mentions where Dr. Ortiz grew up in order to:
options: prove the wells were safe during Dr. Ortiz's childhood
suggest that Dr. Ortiz has a personal stake in the results
explain why Dr. Ortiz tested 40 wells and not more of them
show that Dr. Ortiz was not qualified to test the wells
C.why: Placing her childhood well among those tested signals a personal connection to the findings. That is the most strongly supported reason for including the detail.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the passage says anything about water quality during her childhood.
whyNot.2: Where she grew up has no stated link to the number of wells tested.
whyNot.3: Nothing questions her qualifications; a personal connection does not imply a lack of skill.

C.q:
Read the passage.

After Brookside Clinic began offering appointments until 8 p.m., the number of missed appointments fell by about a third. Most of the new evening slots were booked by patients who work daytime jobs.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
options: Missed appointments led the clinic to end its daytime hours.
Patients with daytime jobs seldom miss evening appointments.
Evening appointments cost the clinic less than daytime ones.
Daytime jobs had kept some patients from attending.
C.why: Missed visits dropped once evening slots opened, and working patients took most of those slots. The best-supported inference is that daytime jobs had been keeping some patients from their appointments.

whyNot.0: Distortion: the clinic added evening hours; nothing says daytime hours ended.
whyNot.1: Overreach: the passage reports a drop in missed visits overall, not the attendance record of working patients in particular.
whyNot.2: Costs are never mentioned, so this has no support in the text.

C.q:
Read the passage.

The sign on the community pool's gate read 'Closed for repairs until further notice.' Behind the fence, the pool held no water, and two workers knelt on its floor, patching long cracks. A stack of new tiles sat beside the diving board.

Which statement is most strongly supported by the passage?
options: The pool was drained so its floor could be repaired.
The pool will reopen to swimmers within the next week.
The pool closed after a swimmer was injured on a crack.
The diving board is being replaced with a set of tiles.
C.why: An empty pool, workers patching cracks on the floor and a sign saying 'closed for repairs' together strongly support that it was drained for floor repairs.

whyNot.1: Possible but unsupported: the sign says 'until further notice', which gives no reopening date.
whyNot.2: No injury is mentioned; this invents a cause the text does not give.
whyNot.3: Distortion: the tiles sit beside the diving board; nothing says they replace it.

reteach.title: Think like a detective
reteach.question: A detective finds muddy boot prints leading from the back door to the kitchen and an open, empty cookie jar. How is the detective's thinking like answering a TEAS inference question?

blocks.body: A good detective does not say 'the butler did it' because butlers often do (outside knowledge). Nor does she say 'someone came in the back door' and stop, because that is simply what the prints show (stated). She reasons: muddy prints from outside, straight to an empty jar, means someone came in from outside and took the cookies. That conclusion uses every clue and contradicts none. TEAS inferences work the same way.

steps.label: Clue
steps.sub: Muddy prints from the back door

steps.label: Clue
steps.sub: Empty cookie jar in the kitchen

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.sub: Prints lead straight to the jar

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.sub: Someone came in and took the cookies

blocks.text: 'It could be true' is not enough. A detective who accuses someone with no clues pointing to them gets the case thrown out.

explain.body: An inference is a conclusion reached by combining evidence in the text with reasoning. It is not written in the text, but the text must support it.

test.q:
Read the passage.

The grocery store's shelves of bottled water, batteries and bread were nearly bare by noon, and the parking lot was full. A radio inside the store was tuned to a weather station.

Which is the best inference?
options: The store had forgotten to order enough water and bread that week.
Shoppers were preparing for a storm that had been forecast.
The store sells more batteries than any other product it stocks.
The radio station had told listeners to shop at that store.
test.why: Water, batteries and bread selling out, a full lot and a radio on a weather station together point to people stocking up before forecast bad weather.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests an ordering problem; a full parking lot points to high demand.
whyNot.2: Overreach: the passage describes one morning, not overall sales.
whyNot.3: Nothing says the station mentioned this store.

explain.body: Clues come from actions, details included or left out, word choice and tone. A character's actions often reveal a feeling the text never names.

head: Clue
Suggests
rows: Checks the clock again and again

test.q:
Read the passage.

Tomas read the lab results twice, folded the paper carefully and let out a long breath. Then he called his sister, laughing as he told her the news.

What can the reader infer about the results?
options: They were worse than Tomas had expected.
They were confusing and hard to read.
They were a relief to Tomas.
They were meant for his sister.
test.why: A long breath out, then laughing while sharing the news, signals relief: the results were good news to him.

whyNot.0: Laughing as he shares the news does not fit bad news.
whyNot.1: Reading twice could suggest care, but his relieved reaction does not fit confusion.
whyNot.3: He told his sister the news; nothing says the results were hers.

explain.body: Inference items also ask why a detail is included, what a phrase suggests or who the reader is. Look at what the detail does in context: does it build trust, give an example, show contrast?

test.q:
Read the passage.

The article on safe lifting at work quotes Ray Delgado, who spent 25 years as a warehouse supervisor before training as a physical therapist. Delgado says most back injuries he has seen came from twisting while lifting.

The author most likely includes Delgado's background in order to:
options: show that warehouse work is more dangerous than therapy
explain why Delgado decided to leave the warehouse
suggest that Delgado's advice comes from experience
argue that supervisors should train as therapists
test.why: Twenty-five years supervising lifting plus therapy training tells readers his advice is grounded in experience, which makes his claim more credible.

whyNot.0: The passage never compares the danger of the two jobs.
whyNot.1: His reasons for changing careers are not discussed.
whyNot.3: No recommendation about supervisors is made or implied.

explain.body: Several options may be possible. Choose the one the details require or most strongly support, and reject anything extreme, unsupported or reversed.

test.q:
Read the passage.

The bakery's display case was full at 7 a.m. By 9 a.m., the blueberry muffins were gone, while every tray of bran muffins was still full.

Which statement is most strongly supported?
options: Customers that morning preferred blueberry to bran.
The bakery will stop baking bran muffins later this month.
Bran muffins cost more at this bakery than blueberry ones.
Blueberry muffins are the best-selling item at every bakery.
test.why: One tray emptied while the other stayed full during the same two hours, so customers that morning picked blueberry over bran.

whyNot.1: A prediction about the bakery's plans is not supported by one morning's sales.
whyNot.3: Extreme: one bakery on one morning says nothing about every bakery.
